ocar.opportunity: Two-sample tests for graphs would let neuroscientists ask whether two connectomes were generated by the same latent structure, not just whether they look similar by eye.
ocar.challenge: Unlike a classical two-sample test with a fixed-dimensional parameter, here the parameter dimension grows with the number of vertices, so ordinary Euclidean tests do not apply.
ocar.action: Tang, Athreya, Sussman, Lyzinski, Park, and Priebe, in the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics (2017), propose a spectral test for whether two finite-dimensional random dot product graphs on a common vertex set share the same generating latent positions, or positions related by a scale or diagonal transform.
ocar.resolution: The test statistic is a function of a spectral decomposition of each adjacency matrix and is argued to be valid and consistent across a broad range of alternatives. Applied to a test–retest neural-connectome dataset it distinguished scans from different subjects; applied to the C. elegans connectome it distinguished chemical from electrical networks, showing power even at small sample size.
ocar.future_work: The paper closes by relating the procedure to generalized likelihood-ratio tests; the extract does not report a follow-up experimental program beyond that comparison and supplementary materials.

summaries.beginner: Scientists often want to know whether two brain wiring diagrams really come from the same kind of network. This statistics paper gives a test for that question and uses it to tell people apart from their connectome scans and to tell chemical from electrical wiring in the worm.
summaries.intermediate: Tang, Athreya, Sussman, Lyzinski, Park, and Priebe (Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2017) formulate a semiparametric two-sample test for random dot product graphs on a shared vertex set. The null is that the latent positions are the same, or related by a scale or diagonal transformation; the statistic is built from spectral decompositions of the two adjacency matrices. They apply the test to a test–retest neural-connectome dataset, where it distinguishes subjects, and to C. elegans chemical versus electrical networks, which they present as evidence of power at small sample size.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract is front matter, abstract, a truncated introduction, and the reference list; numerical p-values, sample sizes of the MRI dataset, and the precise form of the test statistic are not in the extract. Claims of distinguishing subjects and chemical versus electrical worm networks are those stated in the abstract. “Consistency” is the paper’s technical notion for this growing-dimension setting, not a claim of unlimited power. Supplementary materials are referenced but not included here.

plain_language_summary: Scientists often want to know whether two brain wiring diagrams really come from the same kind of network. This statistics paper gives a test for that question and uses it to tell people apart from their connectome scans and to tell chemical from electrical wiring in the worm.

ocar.opportunity: A complete wiring diagram of a large brain would need maps at many spatial scales at once, like a Google Earth view of continents down to streets.
ocar.challenge: Medical imaging, light microscopy, and electron microscopy each show only part of that hierarchy, and current pipelines cannot finish a large-animal brain within a typical research career. Electron microscopy could in principle reconstruct all synapses, but not as a practical whole-brain path for large animals in the foreseeable future.
ocar.action: Hwu, Margaritondo, and Chiang, in a BMC Biology Q&A (2017), argue for synchrotron x-ray tomography as an in situ, multi-scale alternative, motivated by their effort to map the whole-body Drosophila connectome after a 2016 Society for Neuroscience Presidential Lecture.
ocar.resolution: They present synchrotron x-rays as bright, deeply penetrating, and tunable from large regions down toward synapses, with volumes that can be aligned to confocal and two-photon functional data. After more than a decade of performance improvements they call x-ray imaging the technique of choice for whole-body connectome mapping, with a proof-of-concept synchrotron imaging effort and a proposed X-ray Connectome Consortium.
ocar.future_work: The piece treats remaining gains in contrast, specimen size, and resolution as still required for whole-brain human-scale work; it is advocacy and methods framing, not a released whole-brain x-ray connectome.

summaries.beginner: Mapping a whole brain at every zoom level is still too slow with today’s main imaging tools. This Q&A argues that synchrotron x-ray tomography could scan an entire animal at many scales and line up with living optical images.
summaries.intermediate: Hwu, Margaritondo, and Chiang (BMC Biology, 2017) answer why synchrotron x-ray tomography belongs in multi-scale connectomics. They contrast region-level medical imaging, cellular light microscopy, and synaptic electron microscopy, and they argue that feasible x-ray improvements could change career-scale feasibility for large brains. The practical driver is whole-body Drosophila mapping: synchrotron sources supply brightness and penetration for in situ volumes that can be registered to confocal and two-photon data. They report more than a decade of work to handle large specimens with usable contrast and tunable resolution, and they close by pointing to an X-ray Connectome Consortium.
summaries.advanced: This is a Q&A opinion piece, not a methods paper with reconstruction completeness statistics. “Technique of choice for whole-body connectome mapping” is the authors’ view. The extract’s proof-of-concept sentence is truncated, so no voxel size, synapse count, or Drosophila completeness figure is taken from the PDF body. Human-scale completeness remains prospective. PMC/BMC open-access copy.

plain_language_summary: Mapping a whole brain at every zoom level is still too slow with today’s main imaging tools. This Q&A argues that synchrotron x-ray tomography could scan an entire animal at many scales and line up with living optical images.

ocar.opportunity: Two-photon imaging can follow neurons, glia, and vessels in living mice, but intact skull scattering blocks synaptic-resolution views of cortex without a cranial window.
ocar.challenge: Open-skull glass windows can inflame the brain for weeks, and thinned-skull windows need repeated grinding as bone regrows. Prior in vivo skull-clearing attempts did not reach synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Zhao, Yu, Zhang, Li, Luo, Xu, and Zhu, in Light: Science & Applications (online 2018; DOI 2017), introduce a skull optical clearing window (SOCW) that uses topical reagents on the intact skull, then two-photon imaging, in living mice.
ocar.resolution: SOCW allowed repeated imaging of neurons, microglia, and microvasculature in superficial cortex. They used it to follow dendritic-spine plasticity in critical periods and to visualize dendrites and microglia after laser ablation, and they report little inadvertent damage or inflammation compared with conventional windows. Imaging depth is limited to the first 250 μm below the pial surface because the skull remains in place.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the method as easier and safer than craniotomy or repeated thinning, while acknowledging that depth cannot match traditional open-skull windows; broader adoption depends on that depth–safety trade-off.

summaries.beginner: Looking at living mouse cortex usually means cutting or grinding the skull. This team paints clearing chemicals on the bone instead, and can watch synapses, immune cells, and tiny blood vessels through it.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao, Yu, Zhang, Li, Luo, Xu, and Zhu (Light: Science & Applications, 2018 version of a 2017 DOI) describe a skull optical clearing window for in vivo two-photon imaging. Reagents are applied to the exposed skull without much thinning or removal. Combined with two-photon microscopy, the window supported repeated views of dendritic protrusions, microglia processes, and capillaries in superficial mouse cortex, plus spine-plasticity and laser-injury experiments. The conclusions stress easier handling and low inflammation, with imaging depth limited to the first 250 μm below the pia because the skull remains.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2017; the PDF is the 2018 Light: Science & Applications article (7, 17153) with the same DOI. Depth “first 250 μm below the pial surface” is stated in the conclusions. The publisher blurb names collagenase, EDTA disodium, and glycerol as agents; those names are not independently re-counted from the truncated methods. Safety is the authors’ claim of little inflammation, which they argue makes the method suitable for microglia. Not a connectome reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Looking at living mouse cortex usually means cutting or grinding the skull. This team paints clearing chemicals on the bone instead, and can watch synapses, immune cells, and tiny blood vessels through it.

ocar.opportunity: Hackathon-style neuroscience meetings generate tools and datasets that traditional conference proceedings, which triage papers before the meeting, are poorly designed to capture.
ocar.challenge: Brainhack events are built so that content emerges on site; an inverted publication form is needed to mark what was actually achieved rather than what was submitted in advance.
ocar.action: Craddock, Bellec, Margulies, Nichols, Pfannmöller, and many contributors publish the 2015 Brainhack Proceedings as GigaScience meeting abstracts (2016), covering three-day events in Honolulu, Montréal, and eight sites across the Americas.
ocar.resolution: The volume is a table of short abstracts (I1 plus A1–A23) on open-science infrastructure: Brainspell curation, NiData, BIDS in C-PAC, AFNI centrality maps, LORIS anonymization, Nipype wrapping of HCP pipelines, CBRAIN, DueCredit, ENIGMA wrappers, NIDM, DIPY tissue classification, and related utilities. It documents a community’s outputs rather than a single experiment.
ocar.future_work: The introduction frames Brainhack as an ongoing conference model for open neuroscience; individual abstracts imply continued software and data-sharing work rather than a unified follow-up study.

summaries.beginner: This is not one experiment. It is a stack of short reports from 2015 Brainhack events, where people spent a few days building shared brain-imaging tools and then wrote up what they made.
summaries.intermediate: The 2015 Brainhack Proceedings (GigaScience, 2016) invert the usual conference-proceedings model: content is published after on-site collaboration at events in Honolulu, Montréal, and eight Americas sites. An introduction by Craddock and colleagues is followed by abstracts A1–A23 spanning annotation (Brainspell), data standards (BIDS/C-PAC, NIDM), pipelines (HCP Minimal Preprocessing in Nipype, AFNI degree centrality), platforms (CBRAIN, LORIS), and analysis libraries (Nitime, DIPY). The piece is a community snapshot of open neuroinformatics, not a single result.
summaries.advanced: Treat this as a supplement of meeting abstracts. The PDF extract covers the introduction and the start of A1; later abstracts are listed in the catalog table of contents but are not fully present in the selected text. Do not attribute a unified empirical finding to the volume. Author-list spelling in the catalog (e.g. “Lune P Bellec”, “Margules”) differs from PDF “Pierre Bellec” / “Margulies”.

plain_language_summary: This is not one experiment. It is a stack of short reports from 2015 Brainhack events, where people spent a few days building shared brain-imaging tools and then wrote up what they made.

ocar.opportunity: If memories are Hebbian cell assemblies in sparsely wired cortex, changing which synapses exist—not only how strong they are—could raise the fraction of required connections that are actually present.
ocar.challenge: Adult learning theories still center on weight change, while experiments show synapse formation and elimination, spine turnover, and axonal/dendritic remodeling whose computational role is not settled.
ocar.action: Knoblauch and Sommer, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2016), define effectual connectivity as the fraction of synaptically linked neuron pairs within a memory-encoding cell assembly, and they study it with theory, simulation, and a simplified structural-plasticity model.
ocar.resolution: They argue that effectual connectivity tracks information storage capacity and is closely related to imaging measures of effective connectivity such as transfer entropy, while remaining anatomically defined. A simplified plasticity model can produce forgetting and an optimal inter-session gap (spacing), with example fits at pe|0 = 0.01 and pd|0 = 0.0002, but the simple model’s optimal gap does not grow with retention interval as in Cepeda et al. (2008) unless synapse populations with different rates are mixed.
ocar.future_work: They suggest using the anatomical–functional link to predict which cortical areas should show ongoing structural plasticity during particular tasks, and they note that mixing synapse populations is needed to match the retention-interval dependence of spacing.

summaries.beginner: Memories may depend not only on stronger synapses but on growing new ones in the right places. This theory paper defines how completely a memory’s neurons are wired to each other and uses that idea to explain why spaced practice can help learning.
summaries.intermediate: Knoblauch and Sommer (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2016) treat structural plasticity as a way to raise effectual connectivity—the fraction of required synapses that exist inside a Hebbian cell assembly. Theory and simulations link that fraction to network storage capacity and to effective-connectivity measures used in imaging. Applying the model to realistic cortical sparsity, they discuss how many assemblies a macrocolumn could hold, and they reduce structural plasticity to a form that can be simulated at larger scale. In that reduced model, faster weight and structural turnover shrinks the optimal gap between learning sessions; a single-population version cannot reproduce Cepeda and colleagues’ finding that the optimal gap grows with retention interval.
summaries.advanced: This is hypothesis-and-theory, not new anatomy. The extract cites potential connectivity Ppot ≈ 0.5 from Stepanyants et al. (2002) rather than measuring it here. Improved estimates of the number of cell assemblies per macrocolumn are claimed in the abstract but the numerical estimate is not in the selected text, so it is not restated. Spacing-effect parameters pe|0 and pd|0 are simulation settings; “data not shown” is attached to the best-fit pair. Model A versus B differ in whether deconsolidation implies synapse elimination.

plain_language_summary: Memories may depend not only on stronger synapses but on growing new ones in the right places. This theory paper defines how completely a memory’s neurons are wired to each other and uses that idea to explain why spaced practice can help learning.

ocar.opportunity: If the brain is a complex network, silencing one well-connected region should change coupling far beyond its direct targets, and a structural connectome should predict those remote effects.
ocar.challenge: Focal neuropathology is hard to map onto distributed functional MRI changes without a causal perturbation and an independent structural graph.
ocar.action: Grayson, Bliss-Moreau, Machado, Bennett, Shen, Grant, Fair, and Amaral, in Neuron (2016), pharmacogenetically inactivate the rhesus monkey amygdala with DREADDs and measure resting-state functional connectivity MRI, then simulate amygdala disconnection on an experimentally established structural connectome.
ocar.resolution: Amygdala inactivation disrupted amygdalocortical communication and corticocortical coupling across multiple systems. Graph-theoretic communication along mono- and polysynaptic paths largely accounted for endogenous correlations and many non-local changes after inactivation. Subjects were four adult male rhesus macaques (mean 5.25 years).
ocar.future_work: Limitations named in the extract include nuclei-level transfection variability, missing subcortical structural data beyond the amygdala, use of static communicability rather than a generative activity model, group-averaged FC matrices, and anesthesia; they suggest awake recordings and generative lesion simulations as next steps.

summaries.beginner: Turning off one brain region can change conversations among many others. In monkeys, silencing the amygdala scrambled widespread fMRI coupling, and a wiring map of the monkey brain helped predict those distant effects.
summaries.intermediate: Grayson and colleagues (Neuron, 2016) inactivated the rhesus amygdala with an inhibitory DREADD (rAAV5/hSyn-hM4D-mCherry) in four adult male macaques and compared resting-state fMRI coupling with graph analysis of experimentally established structural connectivity. Inactivation disrupted amygdalocortical communication and distributed corticocortical coupling. Simulated disconnection, using communicability through mono- and polysynaptic paths, accounted for much of the endogenous correlational structure and many remote functional changes. The discussion flags nuclei-specific transfection, sparse subcortical structural data, non-generative communicability, group-averaged matrices, and anesthesia as limits on how far the mapping can be pushed.
summaries.advanced: N = 4 males; results should not be read as a large-N or female-inclusive primate sample. Literature values 0.6 < r < 0.7 are cited for prior corticocortical structure–function prediction, not as this paper’s reported fit. The PDF is an NIH author manuscript. “Largely accounted for” is the authors’ qualitative summary; a single scalar fit is not taken from the extract. DREADD inactivation is not a surgical lesion, so residual amygdala activity is possible.

plain_language_summary: Turning off one brain region can change conversations among many others. In monkeys, silencing the amygdala scrambled widespread fMRI coupling, and a wiring map of the monkey brain helped predict those distant effects.

ocar.opportunity: Locomotion and other behavioral states strongly modulate mouse V1, and a popular account is a Vip→Sst disinhibitory motif that releases pyramidal cells.
ocar.challenge: If that motif were the whole story, locomotion should suppress Sst when it excites Vip, and vice versa; cell-type recordings might not obey that pattern once stimulus size is taken into account.
ocar.action: Dipoppa, Ranson, Krumin, Pachitariu, Carandini, and Harris, in a bioRxiv preprint (posted 2016; extract is the 18 July 2017 version), image pyramidal, Vip, Sst, and Pvalb cells in layer 2/3 of mouse V1 during vision and locomotion and fit a circuit model that can retune synaptic weights with behavioral state.
ocar.resolution: With large stimuli, locomotion increased Sst responses without suppressing Vip cells; with small stimuli, it increased Vip responses without suppressing Sst cells. A model could reconstruct each type’s activity from the others only if locomotion increased feedforward weights and also modulated recurrent weights, arguing against disinhibition as the sole mechanism.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s later pages are methods and acknowledgments rather than a dedicated outlook; the scientific implication left standing is that locomotion should be modeled as a change in effective synaptic connectivity, not only as a Vip–Sst switch.

summaries.beginner: Running changes how mouse visual cortex responds to what the eyes see. This study finds that the popular “VIP cells shut off SST cells, which frees excitatory cells” story is too simple: which inhibitory cells speed up depends on whether the visual stimulus is large or small.
summaries.intermediate: Dipoppa, Ranson, Krumin, Pachitariu, Carandini, and Harris (bioRxiv, 2016 paper; July 2017 version in the extract) record layer 2/3 pyramidal, Vip, Sst, and Pvalb neurons in mouse V1. The canonical disinhibitory circuit (Vip inhibits Sst, thereby disinhibiting pyramids) fails to match the locomotion effects they measure: large stimuli plus running raise Sst without suppressing Vip, whereas small stimuli plus running raise Vip without suppressing Sst. Their circuit model fits the observed activity of each type from the others only when locomotion can increase feedforward synaptic weights and modulate recurrent weights. The conclusion is that behavioral state changes effective connectivity, not merely a disinhibitory switch.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint (CC-BY-NC-ND), not the later journal version if one exists; statements follow this extract. The discussion section in the selected text is not captured (methods, fitting, and acknowledgments occupy the tail). Quantitative tuning curves, animal N, and which single-synapse change best explained locomotion are in supplements referenced as Supplementary Figure 16, not restated here. Pvalb cells are recorded but the abstract’s main contrast is Vip/Sst versus the disinhibitory model.

plain_language_summary: Running changes how mouse visual cortex responds to what the eyes see. This study finds that the popular “VIP cells shut off SST cells, which frees excitatory cells” story is too simple: which inhibitory cells speed up depends on whether the visual stimulus is large or small.

ocar.opportunity: The WU-Minn Human Connectome Project needed a public archive that could house multimodal MRI and MEG plus behavior, and deliver terabyte-scale downloads to a worldwide user base.
ocar.challenge: Open imaging data mix unrestricted images with sensitive behavioral fields, and naive HTTP transfer cannot move petabyte-scale packages reliably.
ocar.action: Hodge, Horton, Brown, Herrick, Olsen, Hileman, McKay, Archie, Cler, Harms, Burgess, Glasser, Elam, Curtiss, Barch, Oostenveld, Larson-Prior, Uğurbil, Van Essen, and Marcus, in NeuroImage (2016 version of a 2015 paper), describe ConnectomeDB as a customized XNAT instance with a web UI, Aspera fasp downloads, hard-drive shipment, and Amazon S3.
ocar.resolution: The database holds structural, task, resting-state, and diffusion MRI plus resting and task MEG, as unprocessed, minimally preprocessed, and analysis derivatives, with open access after data-use terms and a stricter tier for sensitive behavior. As of April 2015 the authors report over a million package files totaling nearly 1.5 petabytes served to over 1900 users in 57 countries, 168 Connectome-In-A-Box requesters, 431 drives shipped, nearly 350 approved restricted-data users, and over 50 publications using released HCP data and methods.
ocar.future_work: Planned work includes further subject releases, diffusion tractography and parcellated task-fMRI derivatives, in-database mining tools, and becoming the NIH Connectome Coordination Facility platform for disease and lifespan HCP-style studies.

summaries.beginner: The Human Connectome Project needed a public warehouse for huge brain-scan files and the tests that go with them. ConnectomeDB is that warehouse: a website, fast downloads, and even mailed hard drives.
summaries.intermediate: Hodge and colleagues (NeuroImage, 2016; DOI 2015) present ConnectomeDB (https://db.humanconnectome.org) as the public XNAT-based archive of the WU-Minn HCP. It stores multimodal MRI (structural, task, rest, diffusion) and MEG (rest and task) at unprocessed, minimally preprocessed, and analysis levels, plus behavior, with open imaging after data-use terms and restricted access to sensitive fields. Delivery uses a guided web UI, Aspera fasp, Connectome-In-A-Box drives, and Amazon S3. Usage statistics in the extract are those as of April 2015 (about 1.5 PB to >1900 users in 57 countries). The platform is positioned as the future Connectome Coordination Facility front end.
summaries.advanced: Usage numbers are a April 2015 snapshot from the author manuscript, not a current census. “Over 50 publications” includes consortium and independent papers since the Q1 release (March 2013) as stated by the authors. This paper describes informatics, not a new connectome analysis. Catalog year 2015 versus published NeuroImage 2016 pagination (124:1102–1107) reflects the DOI date. PDF is an NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: The Human Connectome Project needed a public warehouse for huge brain-scan files and the tests that go with them. ConnectomeDB is that warehouse: a website, fast downloads, and even mailed hard drives.

ocar.opportunity: Major depressive disorder involves several large-scale functional networks, so resting-state connectivity could supply a systems-level picture of the illness.
ocar.challenge: Seed-based and ICA studies of depression do not all agree, and findings need to be placed inside existing hypotheses of network dysfunction rather than listed as isolated edges.
ocar.action: Mulders, van Eijndhoven, Schene, Beckmann, and Tendolkar, in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (2015), review resting-state functional connectivity studies of MDD that used seed-based correlation or independent component analysis, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports four relatively consistent patterns: increased connectivity within the anterior default mode network; increased connectivity between the salience network and the anterior default mode network; altered connectivity between anterior and posterior default mode network; and decreased connectivity between the posterior default mode network and the central executive network. The authors treat depression as a network-based disorder.
ocar.future_work: How these four motifs should be tested prospectively, and how much study-level heterogeneity remains, cannot be read from the abstract alone.

summaries.beginner: Depression is not only a chemical story; it also shows up as changed conversations among large brain networks at rest. This review gathers those imaging studies and highlights a few patterns that keep appearing.
summaries.intermediate: Mulders, van Eijndhoven, Schene, Beckmann, and Tendolkar (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 2015) review resting-state fMRI connectivity in major depressive disorder using seed-based correlation or ICA. According to the catalog abstract, despite between-study differences, recurring findings are increased anterior default-mode connectivity, increased salience–anterior default-mode coupling, changed anterior–posterior default-mode coupling, and decreased posterior default-mode–central-executive coupling. Summaries here follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Li, Chen, Chaudhary, Ide, and Li, International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology (2026), on Granger-causality inputs to subgenual cingulate and depressive symptom severity in 890 Human Connectome Project young adults, not the Mulders et al. 2015 review. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews paper is required for study counts, seed choices, and the proposed model.

plain_language_summary: Depression is not only a chemical story; it also shows up as changed conversations among large brain networks at rest. This review gathers those imaging studies and highlights a few patterns that keep appearing.

ocar.opportunity: Aligning two graphs so that edge disagreements are minimized is a core step in connectomics, computer vision, and combinatorics, if it can be solved reliably.
ocar.challenge: Exact graph matching is computationally hard. Practitioners relax the discrete permutation search to a continuous problem for gradient methods, but few relaxations have guarantees, and a popular convex relaxation may be the wrong one.
ocar.action: Lyzinski, Fishkind, Fiori, Vogelstein, Priebe, and Sapiro, in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (2015; arXiv 2014–2015), compare an indefinite relaxation of graph matching with a common convex relaxation.
ocar.resolution: They prove that an indefinite relaxation, when solved exactly, almost always recovers the optimal permutation, whereas a common convex relaxation almost always fails to do so. Theory suggests initializing the indefinite algorithm at the convex optimum; experiments on benchmarks and real data support combining the two.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is references rather than an outlook section; the practical recommendation left standing is to amalgamate convex initialization with indefinite refinement rather than trusting convex relaxation alone.

summaries.beginner: Matching two networks so that the same nodes line up is a notoriously hard puzzle. This paper shows that a popular “make it convex so it is easy” shortcut usually misses the right alignment, and a less tidy relaxation does better.
summaries.intermediate: Lyzinski, Fishkind, Fiori, Vogelstein, Priebe, and Sapiro (IEEE TPAMI; arXiv:1405.3133v3, 10 Jan 2015) study graph matching: minimize the Frobenius disagreement ||A − PBPᵀ||_F over permutation matrices P. They prove that an indefinite continuous relaxation almost always yields the optimal permutation when solved exactly, while a common convex relaxation almost always does not. The recommended heuristic is to start the indefinite solver from the convex optimum. Experiments on benchmark and real problems are cited as corroboration. Connectomics is named as an application domain alongside vision and combinatorics.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2014; the PDF is an arXiv v3 manuscript corresponding to the TPAMI article (DOI 2015). “Almost always” is the paper’s probabilistic language for the stated random-graph setting, not a guarantee on every connectome. The selected extract does not include numerical accuracy tables. Other matching objectives exist; this paper focuses on the Frobenius/permutation formulation. No new biological reconstruction is presented.

plain_language_summary: Matching two networks so that the same nodes line up is a notoriously hard puzzle. This paper shows that a popular “make it convex so it is easy” shortcut usually misses the right alignment, and a less tidy relaxation does better.

ocar.opportunity: Recovery after brain damage, and the ability to resect eloquent-looking cortex without lasting deficit, are hard to explain if adult function is strictly modular and static.
ocar.challenge: A localizationist map of fixed critical regions does not account for postoperative recovery or for remapping seen when the same patient is operated on more than once.
ocar.action: Duffau, in Cortex (2014), reviews serial mappings in patients who underwent awake surgery for diffuse glioma infiltrating eloquent structures, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports three strands: intraoperative cortical and subcortical electrical mapping that supports a network view of language and other functions; pre/post neuropsychological and functional imaging evidence that large resections of supposedly critical cortex can spare lasting sequelae via circuit reorganization; and remapping across repeated surgeries for tumor relapse. White-matter connectivity is presented as the main limit on that plastic potential.
ocar.future_work: A better connectomic account of which subcortical pathways are indispensable is the implied constraint on how far adult reorganization can go; details are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Adult brains can reroute function after injury more than old modular maps suggest. This surgical review argues that glioma operations done awake show that plasticity, not a fixed list of “untouchable” spots, often keeps language and thought going—until key white-matter cables are cut.
summaries.intermediate: Duffau (Cortex, 2014) uses serial mappings from awake glioma surgery to argue against a static localizationist model of adult brain function. According to the catalog abstract, intraoperative cortical and subcortical stimulation supports network-level organization (including language), combined neuropsychology and functional imaging show that large resections of “critical” cortex can avoid permanent sequelae through reorganization, and repeated operations document remapping in the same patients. The limiting factor emphasized is white-matter connectivity: extensive subcortical damage is what blocks recovery. Summaries here follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Forkel, Dulyan, Schilling, and Thiebaut de Schotten, Brain Structure and Function (2026), a review on neurovariability as adaptive brain function, not Duffau’s 2014 Cortex paper on glioma surgery and plasticity. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Cortex article is required for case series size, mapping protocols, and which tracts are treated as plastic limits.

plain_language_summary: Adult brains can reroute function after injury more than old modular maps suggest. This surgical review argues that glioma operations done awake show that plasticity, not a fixed list of “untouchable” spots, often keeps language and thought going—until key white-matter cables are cut.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding how large sets of neurons compute requires dense maps of activity and of wiring, not only molecular and single-cell biophysics.
ocar.challenge: In most model organisms those dense measurements are still out of reach; brains are too large for exhaustive optical recording and for EM-scale reconstruction of whole circuits.
ocar.action: Friedrich, Genoud, and Wanner, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2013), review why zebrafish—larval and adult—are well suited for dense activity imaging and large-scale EM reconstructions, with examples from olfactory-bulb computation.
ocar.resolution: They emphasize small brain size as enabling exhaustive optical activity measurements and EM wiring diagrams. In their own EM work, extra- and intracellular membrane contrast lets synapses be identified visually; preliminary comparisons of independent tracings suggest that most disagreements are missed branch points rather than ambiguous image data. The review treats zebrafish as a path to mechanistic circuit analysis and, later, disease and small-molecule screens.
ocar.future_work: Quantitative evaluation of tracing reliability and comparison with higher-resolution EM for synapse identification are described as underway. Translational disease models and behavioral small-molecule screens are presented as emerging uses rather than completed connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Some brains are small enough that scientists can watch almost every cell fire and, in principle, draw almost every wire. This review explains why zebrafish are a leading animal for that kind of complete circuit work, especially in the smell center.
summaries.intermediate: Friedrich, Genoud, and Wanner (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2013) review dense reconstruction of activity and connectivity, then argue that zebrafish offer a rare combination of genetics, transparency, and especially small brain size at both larval and adult stages. Small brains make exhaustive two-photon activity imaging and large-scale EM reconstructions tractable. The authors illustrate the program with olfactory-bulb computations and report that their EM staining yields extra- and intracellular membrane contrast sufficient to identify synapses by eye, with tracing disagreements so far mostly attributable to missed branches rather than image ambiguity. Concluding remarks also flag zebrafish disease models and chemical-genetic screens.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2013 review plus in-progress EM, not a released olfactory-bulb connectome with synapse counts. “Preliminary results” on tracing reliability are explicitly unfinished. Circuit size “typically defined as anatomically distinct networks of 10²–…” is truncated in the extract, so a numeric upper bound is not taken from the PDF. Adult as well as larval small size is part of their pitch, which differs from larva-only zebrafish connectomics narratives.

plain_language_summary: Some brains are small enough that scientists can watch almost every cell fire and, in principle, draw almost every wire. This review explains why zebrafish are a leading animal for that kind of complete circuit work, especially in the smell center.

ocar.opportunity: Graph analyses of human structural and functional connectomes are hard to communicate unless networks can be drawn on a brain surface with controllable nodes and edges.
ocar.challenge: Connectome construction toolboxes (PANDA, BCT, GAT, GRETNA, and others) measure topology but do not provide brain-specific visualization, while general network drawers such as NetworkX and Pajek ignore anatomy.
ocar.action: Xia, Wang, and He, in PLoS ONE (2013), introduce BrainNet Viewer, a MATLAB GUI that renders human connectomes as ball-and-stick models on a brain surface, freely available on NITRC.
ocar.resolution: Users can load combinations of surface, nodes, and edges; adjust color, size, and layout; show multiple views; map volumes onto the surface; export common image formats or videos; and query vertices interactively. The authors demonstrate region-based (including AAL) and voxel-based networks and argue that 3-D anatomical display beats mosaic matrices or planar dot-and-line plots for connectome figures.
ocar.future_work: They position the tool as a visualization platform that might suggest new questions about network organization; dynamic (time-varying) connectomes are mentioned as a batch/video use case rather than a solved analysis.

summaries.beginner: Brain-network papers are full of abstract graphs that are hard to look at. BrainNet Viewer is a free MATLAB program that draws those networks as balls and sticks on a 3-D brain so the anatomy is obvious.
summaries.intermediate: Xia, Wang, and He (PLoS ONE, 2013) present BrainNet Viewer (www.nitrc.org/projects/bnv/), a MATLAB GUI for macro-scale human connectome visualization. It draws brain surface, nodes, and edges in sequence, supports multiple camera views, maps volumetric properties onto the surface, exports stills and videos, and offers interactive zoom, rotate, and data tips. Display properties (color, size, layout) are edited in a settings panel. The discussion contrasts the tool with analysis packages that lack visualization and with generic network drawers that omit neuroanatomy, using AAL as a representative regional atlas while allowing other parcellations.
summaries.advanced: This is software description plus demonstration, not a biological discovery. “Toolboxes for graph-based network visualization are still lacking” is the 2013 claim. AAL is used as a common atlas, not as a claim that it is the correct parcellation. The extract does not report a user study or rendering benchmark. MATLAB dependence is inherent.

plain_language_summary: Brain-network papers are full of abstract graphs that are hard to look at. BrainNet Viewer is a free MATLAB program that draws those networks as balls and sticks on a 3-D brain so the anatomy is obvious.

ocar.opportunity: Stroke often leaves lasting cognitive problems, and new neurons are born after injury, but it has been unclear whether those new cells actually help memory recover.
ocar.challenge: Correlations between neurogenesis and recovery do not prove causation, and ablating progenitors might change infarct size or blood flow rather than connectivity.
ocar.action: Sun, Sun, Wu, Lee, Akamatsu, Wang, Kernie, and Liu, in Journal of Neuroscience (2013), conditionally ablate nestin-expressing neuroprogenitor cells in nestin-δ-HSV-TK-EGFP mice with four weeks of ganciclovir (200 mg/kg/d) before experimental stroke, then test cognition, motor function, and perforant-path connectivity.
ocar.resolution: GCV depleted type 1 and type 2 NPCs in a duration-dependent way without changing peri-infarct astroglia or oligodendrocyte genesis, infarct size, or reperfusion. Transgenic stroke mice on GCV were worse on Barnes-maze acquisition and memory than saline transgenic or GCV-treated wild-type stroke mice, while poststroke motor scores did not differ despite SVZ NPC loss. PRV614 injected in dentate gyrus labeled fewer entorhinal neurons after NPC ablation, consistent with reduced DG–EC synaptic connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats reduced perforant-path connectivity as a candidate explanation for the memory deficit, not a fully isolated mechanism; how SVZ versus hippocampal progenitors contribute, and whether motor tasks are simply less sensitive, remains open in this extract.

summaries.beginner: After a stroke, the brain makes extra new neurons, but do they help thinking come back? In mice, wiping out those progenitor cells made spatial memory recover worse, and a key memory pathway looked less well connected, while walking was not clearly worse.
summaries.intermediate: Sun and colleagues (Journal of Neuroscience, 2013) use nestin-δ-HSV-TK-EGFP mice so that ganciclovir (200 mg/kg/d for 4 weeks before stroke) ablates nestin-expressing type 1 and type 2 neuroprogenitor cells. Ablation did not change infarct size, reperfusion (OCT), or peri-infarct gliogenesis. Cognitive outcome on the Barnes maze was worse in TK+ GCV stroke mice than in TK+ vehicle or TK− GCV stroke controls, whereas gait and ladder-rung motor measures were not significantly different among stroke groups despite SVZ NPC loss. Retrograde PRV614 from dentate gyrus labeled fewer entorhinal neurons after ablation, which the authors link to impaired poststroke memory.
summaries.advanced: Motor n is reported as 18–24/group in the extract; OCT reperfusion uses n = 3–6/group. Cognitive p-values in Figure 6 legends (e.g. p < 0.005 for acquisition) should be read from the figure, not re-derived here. PRV614 is polysynaptic, so “fewer labeled EC neurons” is not a synapse census. Intro statistics on poststroke dementia (~10% new dementia after first-ever stroke; delayed dementia as high as 50%) are cited from Pendlebury and Rothwell, not generated in this experiment. Distal MCA occlusion model.

plain_language_summary: After a stroke, the brain makes extra new neurons, but do they help thinking come back? In mice, wiping out those progenitor cells made spatial memory recover worse, and a key memory pathway looked less well connected, while walking was not clearly worse.

ocar.opportunity: Epilepsy is a disease of abnormal neuronal connections at systems scale; whole-brain and local-circuit mapping tools now exist that ion-channel studies alone cannot substitute for.
ocar.challenge: Mechanisms of epileptogenesis (becoming epileptic) and ictogenesis (producing a seizure) remain incomplete if they stay at channels and transmitters without the aberrant networks that generate hypersynchrony and propagation.
ocar.action: Engel, Thompson, Stern, Staba, Bragin, and Mody, in Current Opinion in Neurology (2013), review connectomic approaches to epilepsy at whole-brain and local-circuit levels.
ocar.resolution: They assign diffusion-tensor MRI to structural whole-brain connectivity, and fMRI plus EEG to functional whole-brain connectivity; optogenetics, tracers, electrophysiology, and calcium imaging address local circuits. The review concludes that delineating aberrant structural and functional connections is now feasible and should inform surgery, comorbidities, and mechanism-based therapy.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion calls for localizing abnormalities in specific syndromes and in individual patients so that surgical targeting and future therapies can be network-based; that program is prospective in this opinion piece.

summaries.beginner: Epilepsy is a problem of how brain cells and regions are wired, not only of single molecules. This review surveys new ways to map those bad connections in the whole brain and in small circuits, with an eye toward better surgery and treatment.
summaries.intermediate: Engel, Thompson, Stern, Staba, Bragin, and Mody (Current Opinion in Neurology, 2013) argue that despite progress on ion channels and transmitters, epilepsy is ultimately a disorder of aberrant neuronal connections. They review DTI for structural whole-brain maps, fMRI and EEG for functional whole-brain maps, and optogenetics, tracers, electrophysiology, and calcium imaging for local circuits. Epileptogenesis and ictogenesis are framed as emergent properties of hypersynchrony and large-scale propagation. The conclusion is that connectomics can now delineate those networks and should guide surgical intervention and research into comorbidities.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative current-opinion review, not a new dataset. No seizure-freedom rates or connectome atlas is introduced here. The PDF is an NIH-PA author manuscript. “Undoubtedly benefit” language in the abstract is prospective. Local-circuit and whole-brain methods are listed as complementary, not as a single pipeline validated in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Epilepsy is a problem of how brain cells and regions are wired, not only of single molecules. This review surveys new ways to map those bad connections in the whole brain and in small circuits, with an eye toward better surgery and treatment.

ocar.opportunity: A project aiming at high-resolution multimodal MRI from each of 1200 people needs industrial-grade quality control, databases, and visualization, not only pulse sequences.
ocar.challenge: Throughput, motion, modality-specific quality, internal operations, and public sharing pull on different informatics designs; visualization of dense connectomes must eventually talk to the database.
ocar.action: Marcus, Harms, Snyder, Jenkinson, Wilson, Glasser, Barch, Archie, Burgess, Ramaratnam, Hodge, Horton, Herrick, Olsen, McKay, House, Hileman, Reid, Harwell, Coalson, Schindler, Elam, Curtiss, Van Essen, and the WU-Minn consortium, in NeuroImage (2013), describe HCP QC procedures, XNAT-based IntraDB and ConnectomeDB, and Connectome Workbench.
ocar.resolution: Primary acquisition and first-order QC are described as stable, while second-order QC, mining, and pipelines (diffusion QC, MEG preprocessing, dense-connectome generation) are still evolving. Custom XNAT features—user agreements, dictionary, dashboard, packages, Aspera, transfer between IntraDB and ConnectomeDB—are being extracted as reusable modules. Workbench can already pull dense connectomes from ConnectomeDB, which the authors call a toehold toward deeper mining of circuits, behavior, heritability, and genetics.
ocar.future_work: They expect better quality-metric cutoffs as N grows, more automated pipelines as methods mature, open-source reuse via Bitbucket, and much tighter Workbench–ConnectomeDB integration for interactive exploration.

summaries.beginner: The Human Connectome Project is as much a software and quality-control operation as a scanner project. This paper describes how the team checks data, stores it, shares it, and looks at it on a 3-D brain workbench.
summaries.intermediate: Marcus and the WU-Minn HCP consortium (NeuroImage, 2013) describe informatics for a planned 1200-subject, high-resolution structural, fMRI, and dMRI resource. QC covers longitudinal consistency, head motion, and modality-specific scores. Internal IntraDB and public ConnectomeDB are customized XNAT services; Connectome Workbench is the visualization environment, already able to remotely open dense connectomes in the database. The discussion states that first-order QC is stable while many second-order tools and pipelines are still in active development, with code on Bitbucket and modules headed to XNAT Marketplace.
summaries.advanced: Written mid-project (3-year acquisition phase dated from August 2010 in the extract). “1200 subjects” is the design goal, not a completed N in this paper. Quality cutoffs are explicitly not yet locked. The NIH author manuscript may differ in pagination from the final NeuroImage 80 issue. This is infrastructure, not a connectivity result.

plain_language_summary: The Human Connectome Project is as much a software and quality-control operation as a scanner project. This paper describes how the team checks data, stores it, shares it, and looks at it on a 3-D brain workbench.

ocar.opportunity: A systematic mouse whole-brain tracer atlas that shows both outgoing and incoming axons from the same injection sites would let olfactory pathways be read as a network, not as isolated tracts.
ocar.challenge: Whether the precise glomerular map in the bulb is preserved in projections to cortex has remained unsettled, and anterior versus posterior piriform cortex may not be equivalent targets.
ocar.action: Hintiryan, Gou, Zingg, Yamashita, Lyden, Song, Grewal, Zhang, Toga, and Dong, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2012), report Mouse Connectome Project double coinjections (one anterograde and one retrograde tracer) into regions of the C57Bl/6J main olfactory bulb, with images in the public iConnectome viewer.
ocar.resolution: Eighteen MOB cases (~72 pathways; 36 efferent and 36 afferent) were available at publication. Analysis supported a topographically arranged MOB projection roadmap, different connectivity of MOB with anterior versus posterior piriform cortex, and mostly lateral rather than medial termination of cortical MOB axons (for example lateral OT, COApl, ENTl). Dorsal/ventral axons occupy different positions in the lateral olfactory tract, matching prior molecular evidence, without a matching spatial arrangement from lot into layer Ia of olfactory cortices in their data.
ocar.future_work: Additional MOB injections and injections of accessory olfactory bulb, anterior olfactory nucleus, and other olfactory cortices were promised as a continuing public release.

summaries.beginner: The mouse smell bulb sends and receives many cables, but those maps used to live in scattered papers. This team injects pairs of tracers, posts the pictures online, and shows that different parts of the bulb follow a topographic road map into smell cortex.
summaries.intermediate: Hintiryan and colleagues (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2012) introduce olfactory connectivity from the UCLA Mouse Connectome Project: double coinjections (anterograde plus retrograde) in C57Bl/6J mice, viewed in iConnectome (www.MouseConnectome.org) against atlas and cytoarchitecture. At publication, 18 main olfactory bulb cases (~72 pathways; 36 each direction) were public. They report a topographic MOB projection roadmap, stronger/denser MOB input to anterior than posterior piriform cortex, and a bias of MOB axons toward lateral divisions of olfactory structures. Lot axons from dorsal versus ventral MOB are stratified, but they did not see a corresponding map from lot into layer Ia.
summaries.advanced: “First open resource for mouse olfactory connectivity data” is the 2012 claim for this MCP product. Pathway count ~72 is the authors’ 18-case inventory, not a complete olfactory connectome. Accessory bulb and AON injections are promised, not delivered in this paper. Interpretation of PIRa versus PIRp differences should be checked against their figures (layer Ia thinning, FG back-label in PIRa not PIRp). Tracer methods do not give synaptic resolution.

plain_language_summary: The mouse smell bulb sends and receives many cables, but those maps used to live in scattered papers. This team injects pairs of tracers, posts the pictures online, and shows that different parts of the bulb follow a topographic road map into smell cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic and large-scale brain connectivity shape neural responses, represent the sensory world, coordinate distributed processing, and store a structural record of the past, which naturally suggests the mathematics of networks.
ocar.challenge: Network science had already transformed other fields, but its contributions to neuroimaging were still being organized; a historical map of the ideas was needed.
ocar.action: Sporns, in NeuroImage (2012), offers a personal perspective on the confluence of networks and neuroimaging, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents the article as a chart of major intellectual themes at the meeting of graph theory and brain imaging, not as a new empirical connectome. Connectivity is treated as fundamental to brain function at multiple scales.
ocar.future_work: What themes the essay flags as unfinished cannot be recovered from the abstract alone.

summaries.beginner: Brain science borrowed the idea of networks from other fields so it could talk about wiring, not only about single regions. This essay looks back at how that way of thinking entered neuroimaging.
summaries.intermediate: Sporns (NeuroImage, 2012) writes a personal perspective on networks in neuroimaging. According to the catalog abstract, connectivity is fundamental to how neurons respond, how the brain represents statistics of the world, how distributed resources are coordinated, and how structure retains a record of the past. Network science, already productive elsewhere, is described as beginning to contribute across neuroscience. The article charts origins of major intellectual themes rather than reporting a new dataset. Summaries here follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Phipps, Whitney, Shou, Torres-Russotto, and Warren on resting-state fMRI of a hypothesized central oscillatory network in orthostatic tremor (Brain Sciences-style article; not the 2012 Sporns NeuroImage essay). Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of Sporns 2012 is required for which historical themes are emphasized.

plain_language_summary: Brain science borrowed the idea of networks from other fields so it could talk about wiring, not only about single regions. This essay looks back at how that way of thinking entered neuroimaging.

ocar.opportunity: Computational models can expose seizure onset and offset mechanisms that are testable in biology, while connectomics can describe the large-scale networks in which those dynamics play out.
ocar.challenge: Human epilepsies are richly described, but mechanisms of seizure start and stop are unknown; animal and slice models generate a bewildering variety of onset mechanisms, and existing computational models are typically too small to be the networks where clinical seizures appear.
ocar.action: Richardson, in Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry (2012), reviews the case for coupling dynamic models of epilepsy with brain connectomics.
ocar.resolution: He emphasizes that seizures emerge rapidly from normal states and usually self-terminate, on a timescale too fast for changes in neuron or process counts, and that even the focal/generalized distinction is not clean. The review concludes that well-developed computational dynamic models and rapidly developing connectomic tools should be married to reveal the abnormal network dynamics that permit seizures.
ocar.future_work: A suggested clinical use is fitting models to a patient to see whether key parameters change after a new treatment, indicating whether the intended mechanism was engaged; that application is prospective.

summaries.beginner: We know many facts about epilepsy but still not why a seizure suddenly starts and stops. This review says the way forward is to put computer models of brain dynamics onto maps of whole-brain wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Richardson (JNNP, 2012) reviews why microscale experimental mechanisms have not yielded a unified account of human seizures. He argues that systems neuroscience—describing and dynamically modeling brain networks—is the missing explanatory level. Three emphases in the extract include the rapid, self-terminating time course of seizures (too fast for anatomical growth or loss of processes), the need to scale simplified computational epilepsy models up to large-scale networks, and connectomics as the description of those networks. The closing claim is that marrying dynamic models with connectomics will be productive for mechanisms and, potentially, for tracking treatment effects in individuals.
summaries.advanced: Commissioned, externally peer-reviewed narrative review, not a new model fit to patients. No specific simulator or connectome dataset is introduced as the author’s own resource. The extract’s middle is truncated; do not invent which neural-mass or coupling model is preferred. BMJ PDF watermark notes a 2026 download date; the article itself is the 2012 review.

plain_language_summary: We know many facts about epilepsy but still not why a seizure suddenly starts and stops. This review says the way forward is to put computer models of brain dynamics onto maps of whole-brain wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome data become scientific only if they can be turned into simulations that check consistency and unknown parameters from local circuits up to interacting brain regions.
ocar.challenge: Local cortical nets of about 10^5 neurons and 10^9 synapses were already routine on clusters, but brain-scale models are orders of magnitude larger, and memory per core on machines such as Blue Gene/P saturates first.
ocar.action: Kunkel, Potjans, Eppler, Plesser, Morrison, and Diesmann, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2012), build a linear model of NEST’s memory use versus network size and core count, then change data structures to exploit sparse local representations of the network.
ocar.resolution: The memory model identifies which software components dominate at which scale and predicts the effect of code changes before implementation. Sparse local structures let NEST scale to the order of 10,000 processors and support simulations on the order of 10^7 neurons and 10^11 synapses on Blue Gene-class hardware; 10^8 neurons and 10^12 synapses are described as realizable with more cores or less overhead for neurons with local targets.
ocar.future_work: Between 10^9 and 10^11 neurons (human-brain order), they expect communication, not memory data structures, to saturate, requiring topology-aware spike routing rather than all-to-all exchange. The memory model does not predict runtime or cache effects of extra indirection.

summaries.beginner: Simulating a whole brain hits a wall when each computer chip runs out of memory. This paper measures that wall in the NEST simulator and changes how wiring is stored so much larger networks can fit on a supercomputer.
summaries.intermediate: Kunkel and colleagues (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2012) argue that before dynamics can test a connectome, simulators must fit meso- and macroscale networks in limited RAM per core. They model NEST memory as a linear function of network size and core count, identify dominant components, and replace dense local tables with structures that exploit sparseness. Prior work (Morrison et al., 2005) had made ~10^5 neurons / 10^9 synapses routine; the new adaptations target ~10^7 neurons / 10^11 synapses on Blue Gene and scaling to ~10,000 processors. Human-brain neuron counts are discussed as a later regime where communication becomes the bottleneck.
summaries.advanced: Neuron/synapse orders of magnitude are the authors’ scaling targets, not a claim that a biologically detailed human model was run. The linear memory model omits runtime. Dedication to Rolf Kötter is in the acknowledgments. NEST is freely available; this paper is about its memory architecture on HPC, not about a particular empirical connectome.

plain_language_summary: Simulating a whole brain hits a wall when each computer chip runs out of memory. This paper measures that wall in the NEST simulator and changes how wiring is stored so much larger networks can fit on a supercomputer.

ocar.opportunity: fMRI and diffusion MRI studies all produce connectivity matrices that are small, graph-ready, and still rich enough to carry individual differences, so a shared repository of matrices could enable meta-analysis across labs.
ocar.challenge: Raw image-sharing archives do not by themselves make graph metrics comparable across modalities, parcellations, and disorders.
ocar.action: Brown, Rudie, Bandrowski, Van Horn, and Bookheimer, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2012), introduce the UCLA Multimodal Connectivity Database, a website for sharing connectivity matrices and running graph-theory reports in the browser.
ocar.resolution: At publication, users had contributed over 2000 individual matrices across fMRI and dwMRI and disorders including Alzheimer’s, autism, and ADHD. A demonstration using 60 adults (ages 26–45) with both resting-state fMRI and dwMRI found low correspondence between global and nodal graph measures of the functional versus structural networks. The site lets users compute metrics, view 2-D/3-D reports, or download raw matrices.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the repository to support larger meta-analyses across modality, age, and disease; that is a stated purpose, not a completed meta-analysis in this methods paper.

summaries.beginner: Many labs end up with a spreadsheet of how strongly every brain region connects to every other. This website lets them post those spreadsheets, run standard network measurements, and compare results across studies.
summaries.intermediate: Brown, Rudie, Bandrowski, Van Horn, and Bookheimer (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2012) describe the UCLA Multimodal Connectivity Database (http://umcd.humanconnectomeproject.org). Connectivity matrices store pairwise connection strengths; the site is both a public CM repository and an in-browser graph-theory analyzer with 2-D and 3-D visualizations. More than 2000 individual CMs had been contributed across fMRI, dwMRI, and several disorders. In a 60-subject (ages 26–45) demonstration, functional and structural whole-brain graph metrics showed low correspondence, which the authors offer as an example of cross-modality comparison the platform is meant to support.
summaries.advanced: “Over 2000” CMs and the 60-subject demo are 2012 snapshot figures; the site may have changed. Low functional–structural correspondence is a result of that demo, not a universal law. URL branding ties the resource to the Human Connectome Project era. This is infrastructure plus a worked example, not a clinical trial. The selected PDF extract is shorter than others (conclusions plus acknowledgments in the tail).

plain_language_summary: Many labs end up with a spreadsheet of how strongly every brain region connects to every other. This website lets them post those spreadsheets, run standard network measurements, and compare results across studies.

ocar.opportunity: Layer 1 sits on a plexus of apical dendrites and long-range axons, so its inhibitory cells are well placed to control dendritic integration in pyramidal neurons—if one knows which L1 types wire to which targets.
ocar.challenge: The interneuronal composition of L1 and its synapses with L2/3 pyramids had not been mapped in comparable detail to deeper-layer microcircuits.
ocar.action: Wozny and Williams, in Cerebral Cortex (2011), classify visually identified L1 neurons in rat somatosensory cortex (postnatal days 24–36) by physiology, anatomy, and unsupervised clustering, and they make simultaneous recordings with L2/3 pyramidal cells.
ocar.resolution: Among 266 L1 neurons they distinguish four Petilla-aligned groups: neurogliaform (n = 72), classical-accommodating (n = 137), fast-spiking (n = 23), and burst-spiking (n = 34). In 384 paired recordings, all L1 groups except neurogliaform cells received monosynaptic excitation from L2/3 pyramids (n = 33 connected observations), with 68 NGFC pairs tested showing no such input. Neurogliaform cells strongly inhibited L2/3 pyramids (12 of 27 pairs). Connectivity and synaptic properties were class-specific.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is references; the implication left in the introduction is that this wiring diagram is a step toward understanding how L1 inhibition sculpts sensory-evoked L2/3 responses, not a full-column connectome.

summaries.beginner: The top layer of rat cortex has several kinds of inhibitory cells, and they do not all plug into the excitatory cells below in the same way. One type (neurogliaform) strongly shuts those cells down but does not get the same return excitation the other types get.
summaries.intermediate: Wozny and Williams (Cerebral Cortex, 2011) study layer 1 interneurons in P24–P36 rat somatosensory cortex. Electrophysiology of 266 visually identified L1 cells, anatomical reconstructions, and unsupervised clustering support four groups matching Petilla classes: neurogliaform (72), classical-accommodating (137), fast-spiking (23), and burst-spiking (34). Simultaneous recordings (n = 384 pairs) with L2/3 pyramids showed class-specific excitation and inhibition: every group except neurogliaform received monosynaptic L2/3 excitatory input, whereas neurogliaform cells provided strong inhibition onto L2/3 pyramids (12/27 pairs) without receiving that excitatory feedback in 68 tested pairs.
summaries.advanced: Counts are those stated in the abstract/opening (266; 72/137/23/34; 384 pairs; 33 excitatory connections onto non-NGFC groups; 68 NGFC pairs without L2/3 EPSPs; 12/27 NGFC→pyramid inhibitory connections). Wistar rats; in vitro slices. “High specificity” is relative to these classes and this layer pair, not a whole-column census. The selected extract does not include the discussion section. Supplementary material is pointed to on the journal site.

plain_language_summary: The top layer of rat cortex has several kinds of inhibitory cells, and they do not all plug into the excitatory cells below in the same way. One type (neurogliaform) strongly shuts those cells down but does not get the same return excitation the other types get.

ocar.opportunity: Digital traces of axons and dendrites turn microscope images into geometry for morphometrics and models, and automation would make that step fast enough for screening and connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Despite many image-processing algorithms, manual tracing remained the dominant way to digitize neuronal morphology, and labs often invent one-off tracers that others never reuse.
ocar.action: Donohue and Ascoli, in Brain Research Reviews (2011 version of a 2010 paper), overview issues in automated reconstruction, survey available techniques, and assess the DIADEM challenge and future prospects.
ocar.resolution: They argue that the best algorithm depends on the biological question and tissue, which encourages custom tools, incompatible formats, and poor reuse. DIADEM showed that generality across datasets is hard: some volumes are harder, algorithms specialize, and there was no clean split between confocal fluorescence and brightfield difficulty. They recommend open-source development, universal data forms, and an archive of existing programs.
ocar.future_work: Standardized definitions and interoperable tools for measuring, modeling, and verifying reconstructions are presented as the route to a healthier ecosystem; fully replacing manual tracing is not claimed as already achieved.

summaries.beginner: Turning a microscope picture of a neuron into a digital stick figure is still mostly done by hand. This review explains why automatic tracing has been slow to take over and what a community contest revealed about the remaining gaps.
summaries.intermediate: Donohue and Ascoli (Brain Research Reviews, 2011; DOI 2010) review digital reconstruction of neuronal morphology from optical microscopy and the state of algorithmic tracing. Automation promises speed, accuracy, and reproducibility needed for high-throughput screening and connectomic data, yet manual tracing remained the overwhelming choice. They discuss the DIADEM challenge: success required generality across diverse datasets; algorithms specialized rather than mapping one-to-one onto datasets, and confocal versus brightfield was not a simple difficulty split. They close by urging open source, shared formats, and documentation so tools are reused rather than reimplemented.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2010/2011 overview, not a new tracer. Catalog year 2010 versus published 2011 pagination (67:94–102) follows the DOI. DIADEM commentary is qualitative in the extract (no leaderboard scores). “To date manual tracing remains the overwhelming choice” is the authors’ contemporary assessment. PDF is an NIH author manuscript. Light-microscopy tracing is the scope; EM connectome pipelines are motivation, not the methods surveyed.

plain_language_summary: Turning a microscope picture of a neuron into a digital stick figure is still mostly done by hand. This review explains why automatic tracing has been slow to take over and what a community contest revealed about the remaining gaps.

ocar.opportunity: If dendritic spines can form and disappear without rebuilding axonal and dendritic arbors, a neuron could switch among many wiring diagrams using only local geometry.
ocar.challenge: The size of that structural-plasticity repertoire is not obvious: it depends on how many nearby axons a dendrite could still connect to, relative to how many synapses it already has.
ocar.action: Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii, in Neuron (2002), define the filling fraction as the ratio of synapses on a dendrite to axons passing within a spine length of that dendrite, and they estimate it from geometry and anatomical data, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports filling fractions of 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus, and an increase by a factor of 1.6–1.8 from macaque V1 to areas V2, V4, and 7a. Because the filling fraction is much smaller than 1, spine remodeling can contribute substantially to structural plasticity without major arbor remodeling.
ocar.future_work: Implications for learning rules and for comparing cortical areas further are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: A dendrite is surrounded by many axons it could touch with a short spine, but it only makes synapses with some of them. This theory paper estimates that leftover “empty slots” are common, so rewiring spines could change circuits a lot without growing new branches.
summaries.intermediate: Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii (Neuron, 2002) quantify how many distinct connectivity patterns are available if spines form and disappear without major arbor remodeling. According to the catalog abstract, that number depends on the filling fraction: synapses on a dendrite divided by axons within a spine length of it. They calculate filling fraction 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus, with a 1.6–1.8-fold increase from macaque V1 to V2, V4, and 7a. Because the ratio is well below 1, spine remodeling is argued to be a large reservoir of structural plasticity. Summaries here follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Rafati, Joca, Vontell, Mallard, Wegener, and Ardalan on a polygamma/actin-cytoskeleton mathematical model of neuronal morphology and electrical activity (2025 dates in the extract), not Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii (Neuron, 2002). Filling-fraction values above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Neuron paper is required for geometrical derivations, species/area samples, and uncertainty on those ratios.

plain_language_summary: A dendrite is surrounded by many axons it could touch with a short spine, but it only makes synapses with some of them. This theory paper estimates that leftover “empty slots” are common, so rewiring spines could change circuits a lot without growing new branches.
